brumadinho-dam-collapse-2019.summary: At 12:28 on 25 January 2019 Dam I at Vale's Córrego do Feijão iron mine near Brumadinho, Minas Gerais, failed by static liquefaction, releasing about twelve million cubic metres of tailings that buried the mine's canteen and offices at lunchtime and swept through Vila Ferteco toward Paraopeba river. Some 270 people died, most of them Vale employees and contractors, three years after Samarco's Fundão dam collapsed at Mariana. An expert panel found the upstream-raised dam steep, saturated and brittle, with no warning before failure; German certifier TÜV SÜD had attested stability months earlier. Brazil banned upstream tailings dams in February 2019 and ordered decommissioning, Vale paid about 37.7 billion reais in a 2021 settlement, and executives faced homicide charges.

colombia-banana-tr4-2019.summary: On 8 August 2019 Colombia's agricultural institute ICA declared a national phytosanitary emergency after laboratories at Wageningen University confirmed Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense tropical race 4 in Cavendish plantations near Riohacha and Dibulla, La Guajira; Resolution 11912 of 9 August set quarantine measures. Soil-borne TR4 kills Cavendish, variety that replaced Gros Michel after race 1 wiped it out in the 1950s, has no cure and persists for decades; it had spread from Asia to Africa and Middle East and now reached a continent that exports most of world's bananas. About 185 to 200 hectares on six farms were destroyed and covered, and Ecuador, Costa Rica and Guatemala tightened border controls. Peru confirmed TR4 in 2021 and Venezuela in 2023.

manaus-oxygen-collapse-2021.summary: On 14 January 2021 hospitals in Manaus, capital of Amazonas, exhausted medical oxygen as COVID-19 admissions far exceeded supplier White Martins's capacity; patients suffocated in wards, families bought cylinders on black markets, and Brazil's air force flew oxygen in while Venezuela sent trucks. A blood-donor study had estimated 76 percent of city residents infected by October 2020, leading some to argue herd immunity had been reached. Genomic surveillance showed a new lineage, P.1 or Gamma, with mutations N501Y, E484K and K417T, emerging in Manaus in November 2020, more transmissible and able to evade antibodies from prior infection. Gamma spread across Brazil and abroad, and a Senate inquiry faulted federal government warnings. Amazonas recorded more than 13,000 deaths.

manaus-oxygen-collapse-2021.detail: Manaus's seroprevalence estimate was later questioned for overestimating attack rate. Its first wave in April and May 2020 had filled mass graves at Parque Tarumã cemetery. In January 2021 daily oxygen demand rose to about 70,000 cubic metres against supply near 28,000. Patients were flown to other states, and Supreme Court ordered federal government to present a plan. Gamma accounted for most Brazilian cases by March 2021 before Delta displaced it.

neom-the-line-announced-2021.summary: On 10 January 2021 Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman unveils The Line in a televised address: a 170 kilometre linear city in NEOM, northwest Saudi Arabia, with no cars, streets or carbon emissions, all daily needs within a five-minute walk and end-to-end transit in twenty minutes. A July 2022 design shows two mirrored walls 500 metres high and 200 metres apart housing 9 million people on 34 square kilometres. Earthworks begin in late 2021 and cost estimates reach into trillions of dollars. In April 2024 Bloomberg reports first phase cut to 2.4 kilometres for under 300,000 residents by 2030, which officials deny before a 2025 strategic review pauses most work. Architects and planners debate it as revival of linear-city ideas and as spectacle for investment.

omicron-identified-2021.summary: Sequencing laboratories in Network for Genomic Surveillance in South Africa, led by Tulio de Oliveira at Stellenbosch and KRISP in Durban, with Botswana's Harvard partnership laboratory, found a SARS-CoV-2 lineage with over thirty spike mutations in samples collected 11 to 16 November 2021, flagged by a PCR target failure in Gauteng. South Africa briefed WHO on 24 November and WHO named B.1.1.529 Omicron, a variant of concern, on 26 November. Within three weeks it was in 87 countries. Rapid, open reporting earned travel bans on southern Africa within hours, which scientists and governments condemned as punishment for surveillance.

Botswana's laboratory sequenced samples from four foreign travellers and Gauteng's Lancet Laboratories noticed S-gene target failure in PCR tests, a marker earlier seen with Alpha. South Africa's government complained that within a day of its announcement, Britain, United States and European Union had banned travel from southern Africa.
